name: Walmart Global Tech
summary: Walmart Global Tech builds the software behind Walmart's stores, e-commerce, supply chain and payments, with tech teams in the US, India (including Bengaluru and Chennai) and elsewhere. Candidates commonly report an online coding test, two or three technical interviews on data structures, design and past projects, and a hiring manager round. Walmart publishes four values, starting with Respect the Individual.
rounds: Online coding assessment for many campus and early-career roles
Technical interviews, often two or three: data structures, problem solving and your projects
System design interview for experienced roles
Hiring manager interview on past work, ownership and teamwork
looks_for: Building for very large scale: many stores, orders and shoppers at once

questions.text: Tell me about a time you listened to an idea from someone junior or outside your team, and it changed your work.
covers: Who suggested it and why it was easy to overlook
How you tested the idea
What changed, and how you credited them

questions.text: Tell me about a time you had to be honest about a mistake or a delay, even though it was uncomfortable.
covers: What went wrong and who it affected
When and how you told them
What you did to fix it and to rebuild trust

questions.text: Tell me about a time you moved quickly but still paid close attention to detail.
covers: Why speed mattered
The details you checked and how
The result and any problem you caught early

questions.text: Tell me about a time you used data to work out what a customer really needed.
covers: The question and the data you used
What surprised you
The decision it led to and the result for customers

questions.text: How would you design a system that shows each store's stock online in near real time?
covers: Stock events from tills, deliveries and returns flowing into one service
Caching for fast reads, and how fresh the numbers need to be
Showing 'low stock' safely when data lags, so shoppers aren't let down

questions.text: How would you design a service that picks the best store or warehouse to fulfil an online order?
covers: Inputs: stock, distance, delivery promise, cost, capacity
Splitting orders across locations, and the trade-offs it brings
Re-routing when a location turns out not to have the item

questions.text: During a big sale, checkout errors suddenly jump. Walk me through how you'd find and fix the problem.
covers: Dashboards first: which step, which service, since when
Recent changes and load on payments, inventory or the database
Quick relief such as rolling back or shedding load, then the real fix

questions.text: Explain the difference between SQL and NoSQL databases, and which you'd choose for a product catalogue.
covers: SQL: fixed schema, joins, strong consistency; NoSQL: flexible schema, easy to scale out
A catalogue's varied product attributes and heavy reads
A reasoned choice, or a mix, with the trade-offs

questions.text: How does caching help a busy shopping website, and what can go wrong with it?
covers: Where caches sit: browser, CDN, application, database
Stale data such as old prices or stock, and how to expire it
Many requests hitting the database at once when a cache entry expires

questions.text: Walk me through a project you built: the design, a hard bug and how you tested it.
covers: The problem and your part
The bug: how you found it and the fix
How you tested it, and what you'd add now

questions.text: Why Walmart Global Tech? What interests you about technology for retail?
covers: Something specific about retail tech: scale, supply chain, stores and online together
How your skills fit the team
What you want to learn

questions.text: Which of Walmart's values do you connect with most, and why?
covers: One value, named once
A short example from your work or studies
How it would show in this role

questions.text: What would you like to learn in your first year here?
covers: Specific skills or systems you want to understand
How you'd go about learning them
How that learning would help the team

tips: Practise talking through data structures and design out loud; interviewers commonly follow your reasoning, not just the answer.
Think at retail scale: many stores, peaks during sales and stock that changes every minute. Bring that into design answers.
Prepare a story for each of Walmart's four values; they're published on its corporate site.
Know your projects deeply; candidates commonly report detailed follow-ups on design choices and testing.
